title: Does Transolver really need a Transformer?

paper.title: Does Transolver really need a Transformer?
paper.abstract:
Abstract The widely used Transolver family of neural operators is based on physics-attention, which softly assigns the points of an unstructured mesh to a small number of
slices, applies self-attention among the resulting tokens, and broadcasts
the result back to the points. We provide a comprehensive empirical and theoretical analysis to elucidate the mechanisms which are responsible for model performance. To this end, we perform careful ablations on a challenging suite of nine 3D fluid dynamics benchmarks to find that replacing token attention with a constant linear map does not affect the accuracy. Thus, Transolver does not need a Transformer at all. However, removing the global mixing (slicing/deslicing) or doing it only once leads to performance collapse. We leverage the theory of averaging neural operators to explain and corroborate our findings by showing that just slicing/deslicing, in conjunction with pointwise MLPs, already suffices for universal approximation of continuous operators and attention is redundant in this context. Finally, we provide a novel FlashAttention-style efficient implementation of the key slicing/deslicing module of Transolver. This
FlashSlice kernel streams slice and deslice over the points without
materializing the heavy slice-weight tensor, while reproducing the best available implementation to floating point error. At the same time, it leads to very significant memory and compute savings, particularly at large slice counts.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Partial differential equations (PDEs) describe diverse phenomena across the physical sciences and engineering ( Evans, 2010 ) , and simulating them accurately is a central task of computational science. Classical numerical methods ( Quarteroni & Valli, 1994 ) do so reliably, but a high-fidelity simulation of a flow around an industrial geometry can occupy an HPC cluster for hours to days. This cost becomes prohibitive in the many-query settings of design optimization, uncertainty quantification and inverse problems, where the same equation is solved for thousands of geometries and operating conditions. Scientific machine learning ( Mishra & Townsend, 2024 ) , in the specific form of operator learning , addresses this bottleneck by learning the solution operator of a PDE from a dataset of simulations, so that a new instance costs a very cheap single forward model pass. The first generation of operator learning algorithms was designed for structured grids: the Fourier neural operator ( Li et al., 2021 ) , DeepONet ( Lu et al., 2021 ) , convolutional neural operators ( Raonić et al., 2023 ) and operator vision transformers ( Herde et al., 2024 ) are based on Cartesian grids. Industrial engineering simulations, however, are based on unstructured meshes and point clouds that can resolve localized features such as boundary layers, shocks and vortices at widely varying point densities. A growing literature targets this setting with graph neural networks ( Pfaff et al., 2021 ; Mousavi et al., 2026 ) , geometry-informed hybrids ( Li et al., 2023b ; Wen et al., 2025 ) and transformers whose tokens are mesh point features ( Cao, 2021 ; Hao et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023a ) . Among the latter, Transolver ( Wu et al., 2024 ) has become a widely used choice. Its physics-attention layer softly assigns each of the N N mesh points to a small number G G of slices , computes self-attention among the G G resulting tokens, and broadcasts the result back to the original points, at a cost linear in N N . It has been extended by Transolver++ ( Luo et al., 2025 ) , Transolver-3 ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) and GeoTransolver ( Adams et al., 2025 ) , among others, and adopted in industrial frameworks such as NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo. Despite its popularity, we argue that the Transolver model itself has not been properly analyzed and understood. In particular, which of its three ingredient operations: slicing/deslicing, attention among the tokens and persistent pointwise MLPs, is responsible for the accuracy shown by the model is completely unclear. Although the focus of successive works on Transolver has been to modify the attention mechanism, it is not even clear whether Transolver really needs a Transformer inside it or not? or whether memory-heavy operations such as slicing/deslicing contribute significantly to its accuracy. Our main motivation for this paper is to perform a comprehensive empirical and rigorous mathematical analysis of the Transolver model to precisely answer such questions. In this regard, our contributions in this paper are, Figure 1: What Transolver’s accuracy does, and does not, need. (a) A Transolver layer: a persistent full-resolution point stream, coupled through slice and deslice with shared per-point slice weights w w to H × G H{\times}G tokens that are re-formed at every layer. Each ablation is drawn on the element it changes; w ( 1 ) w^{(1)} denotes the layer- 1 1 weights reused by FrozenSlice and w ′ w^{\prime} the separate deslice weights of Untied . (b) Validation-error ratio to the full model for the five ablations on nine benchmarks, markers as in (a). The variants that keep the coupling ( NoTokenAttn , Untied , FrozenSlice ) sit at ≈ 1 × \approx 1\times ; removing it ( MlpOnly ) costs 1.04 1.04 – 5.6 × 5.6\times and collapsing the point stream ( SliceOnce ) up to 6.8 × 6.8\times . (c) One reference solution per benchmark family, each beside the rows of (b) it belongs to: Taylor–Green vorticity, and surface pressure with streamlines on SHIFT-Wing, DrivAerNet++, SHIFT-SUV and DrivAerML. • A careful empirical analysis of physics-attention across nine benchmarks (§ 2 – 3 ). We perform controlled ablations of every design decision within the Transolver model, trained under an identical protocol on nine challenging 3D benchmarks (see Fig. 1 ) to demonstrate the surprising fact that replacing token self-attention by a constant linear map matches the full model on all nine ( − 2.6 % -2.6\% to + 7.9 % +7.9\% ) , at every slice count from 8 8 to 256 256 . Moreover, we identify that the slice-deslice operations are essential and removing them leads to significant loss of accuracy, increasing the error by 1.04 1.04 – 5.6 × 5.6\times . Finally, we also show that slicing and deslicing have to be repeated every layer. Not doing so and simply running a deep transformer on the tokens leads to very large drops in accuracy, with errors 2.2 2.2 – 6.8 × 6.8\times those of the baseline model. • A mathematical explanation from the theory of neural operators (§ 4 ). By interpreting slicing/deslicing as finite-rank nonlocal integral operators with a learned partition of unity and leveraging the universal approximation theorem of Lanthaler et al. (2023) , we show that the transformer-free Transolver is already universal, that a purely pointwise stack is bounded away from every nonlocal target at any width and depth, and that slicing/deslicing once is not as efficient as doing it each layer. • FlashSlice (§ 5 ). We implement the key slicing/deslicing module as fused Triton kernels that stream over the points and never write the slice-weight tensor, with a single-tile path for small slice counts and a G G -blocked path with saved softmax statistics for arbitrary ones. They are exact and bit-deterministic, and train 1.35 1.35 – 1.7 × 1.7\times faster in up to 25 % 25\% less memory at the standard configuration over the current implementation and 4 4 – 6.5 × 6.5\times faster in 85 85 – 96 % 96\% less memory at large slice counts. Thus, we provide a comprehensive empirical analysis that identifies the key causal mechanism underlying Transolver’s accuracy, explain it with mathematical theory and provide a highly efficient implementation of this core layer.

The solution operator 𝒮 : X → Y \mathcal{S}:X\to Y , a ↦ u a\mapsto u , is what a neural operator Ψ θ \Psi_{\theta} approximates, given training pairs ( a k , 𝒮 ⁡ ( a k ) ) (a_{k},\mathcal{S}(a_{k})) with a k a_{k} drawn from a distribution μ \mu on X X . sections.heading: The Transolver layer.
sections.text: Transolver ( Wu et al., 2024 ) lifts the per-point inputs to features f i ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ c f_{i}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{c} and applies L L layers, with 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ L 1\leq\ell\leq L , of two interleaved streams. The token stream is physics-attention: per head, a linear projection of the features with a learned temperature τ \tau produces slice weights w i , g = softmax g ​ ( ( W s ​ f i + b ) / τ ) w_{i,g}=\mathrm{softmax}_{g}\big((W_{s}f_{i}+b)/\tau\big) , a soft assignment of each point to G G slices (with layer index ℓ \ell suppressed for notational convenience); the slice operator outputs tokens as weighted averages z g = ∑ i w i , g ​ v i / ∑ i w i , g z_{g}=\sum_{i}w_{i,g}v_{i}/\sum_{i}w_{i,g} of projected features v i v_{i} ; self-attention is applied among the G G tokens; and deslice broadcasts the result back, u i = ∑ g w i , g ​ z g ′ u_{i}=\sum_{g}w_{i,g}z^{\prime}_{g} , added residually to the features. The point stream is a pointwise two-layer MLP with residual connection at full resolution after every attention sublayer, forming a persistent point-level representation. Two properties are worth mentioning: the slice weights are recomputed from the current features at every layer, and the same weights are used in the slice and deslice operators, i.e. they are tied .

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We use nine dataset configurations from CFD, the three-dimensional Taylor–Green vortex which is the prototype of turbulent time-varying flows ( Molinaro et al., 2024 ) and aerodynamics at industrial scale, namely DrivAerNet++ ( Elrefaie et al., 2024 ) surface and volume (fixed inflow), SHIFT-SUV surface and volume (fixed inflow, geometry the only input), the transonic SHIFT-Wing surface and volume (varying inflow and geometry), and DrivAerML ( Ashton et al., 2024 ) surface and volume (fixed inflow; up to 1.3 × 10 8 1.3\times 10^{8} points per sample). The suite spans a very diverse set of operators, ranging from inputs that contain the local field state to solutions set by a global interaction of geometry and operating conditions (Appendix B ).

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: For each benchmark, all variants of Transolver are trained to a common step budget on identical data pipelines with the Transolver backbone of Wu et al. (2024) ( L = 8 L{=}8 , width 256 256 , 8 8 heads, G = 32 G{=}32 ; 3.87 3.87 M parameters); the headline pair Baseline / NoTokenAttn uses three seeds. We report the best validation relative L 1 L^{1} error for each variant. Step budgets are checked rather than assumed and every ablation is verified from the trained artifacts through checkpoint contents and bit-level freeze tests, see Appendix C for details.

sections.heading:
The token self-attention is removable on all nine
benchmarks, i.e., Transolver does not really need a Transformer!
sections.text: We observe from Table 1 that NoTokenAttn , which replaces the content-dependent attention among the G G tokens by a learned linear map applied to each token separately, so that the tokens no longer interact, matches Baseline everywhere: it lies within − 2.6 % -2.6\% to + 1.8 % +1.8\% on seven benchmarks and at + 3.8 % +3.8\% and + 7.9 % +7.9\% on the remaining two (SHIFT-SUV volume and DrivAerML surface), against the 1.04 1.04 – 6.8 × 6.8\times spread of the coupling ablations in the same table, and on four benchmarks it is the best variant overall (tied with Baseline on SHIFT-Wing volume).

sections.heading: Untying the projections is not what makes it removable.
sections.text: A possible explanation of the above result is that tying the slice and deslice projections confines feature interaction to the same token, so that the attention has to supply the missing cross-slice routing. On this reading, untying these projections is what renders attention redundant ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . This explanation and ours (§ 4 ) disagree on the tied and attention-free layer, which Hu et al. (2026) predict to perform poorly, whereas NoTokenAttn already demonstrates that this is not the case. Moreover, in Fig. 2 (a), we present results for the 2 × 2 2\times 2 grid of token attention × \times projection tying on SHIFT-SUV surface, the untied and attention-free cell corresponds exactly to the LinearNO layer of Hu et al. (2026) ported into our scaffold at matched latent width and capacity (Appendix E ). The grid clearly shows that there is no difference between these configurations: all four cells lie within 1.05 % 1.05\% of one another, and both main effects ( + 0.54 % +0.54\% for removing the attention, − 0.51 % -0.51\% for untying) and their interaction ( − 0.41 % -0.41\% ) are about one standard deviation of the baseline’s own three-seed spread of ± 0.47 % \pm 0.47\% . The attention is redundant, and the tying is clearly orthogonal to that redundancy. LinearNO also normalizes its slice weights by a softmax over all points instead of per point, and at its published latent width a training iteration is 6.8 × 6.8\times slower with no change in accuracy (Appendix E ).

sections.heading:
The slice/deslice coupling and the point stream are not
removable.
sections.text: Removing the entire attention sublayer ( MlpOnly ) costs 1.04 × 1.04\times to 5.6 × 5.6\times (Table 1 ). This is not explainable in terms of model capacity: widening the pointwise MLP to 112 % 112\% of the baseline’s parameters ( MlpOnly-Wide , Fig. 2 (c)) recovers at most 3 % 3\% of the gap and leaves the model 1.6 × 1.6\times (surface) and 1.9 × 1.9\times (volume) less accurate on DrivAerNet++. Nor is this difference attributable to budget differences; on SHIFT-SUV the MlpOnly ratio grows from 1.52 × 1.52\times to 1.62 × 1.62\times (surface) and from 2.43 × 2.43\times to 3.24 × 3.24\times (volume) as the budget rises from 10 10 k to 50 50 k steps (Appendix C ). Conversely, SliceOnce keeps the attention and has more parameters than the baseline, but slices once and confines all further depth to the G G tokens; it is the worst variant on every benchmark, at 2.2 2.2 – 6.8 × 6.8\times . On the other hand, re-using the layer- 1 1 slice weights in every layer ( FrozenSlice ) costs only − 0.5 % -0.5\% to + 17 % +17\% , mostly on the volume tasks. Thus, cross-point coupling through slice/deslice, re-estimated at every layer and interleaved at full resolution with the pointwise stream, is clearly the most performant mechanism.

sections.heading: The coupling is needed where the physics is nonlocal.
sections.text: The MlpOnly penalty tracks the physics of each task. It is negligible ( 1.04 × 1.04\times ) on Taylor–Green, whose inputs contain the current field state at every point so that short-horizon prediction is largely local. On the aerodynamic benchmarks the field at a point is set by a global interaction between the whole body and the flow around it, which a function of local descriptors can absorb only in part (Appendix D.1 ), and the size of the penalty does not follow the inflow: it is moderate ( 1.5 1.5 – 3.3 × 3.3\times ) for DrivAerNet++ and SHIFT-SUV and largest for DrivAerML (up to 5.6 × 5.6\times ), all three at fixed inflow, while SHIFT-Wing, the only benchmark whose inflow varies, lies between these ( 2.4 2.4 – 3.2 × 3.2\times ). SHIFT-SUV isolates a second axis, the kind of target: same cars, split, budget and fixed condition, differing only in whether the target is a trace on the body or a field transported away from it, and every coupling-sensitive number roughly doubles from surface to volume ( MlpOnly 1.61 → 3.27 × 1.61\to 3.27\times , SliceOnce 2.87 → 6.79 × 2.87\to 6.79\times ); SHIFT-Wing shows the same changes under varying inflow ( MlpOnly 2.39 → 3.21 × 2.39\to 3.21\times , SliceOnce 2.68 → 6.24 × 2.68\to 6.24\times ). The per-field decomposition makes the same point inside each task (Figure 2 (d)): on every aerodynamic benchmark the pressure, which can be recovered as the solution of a global elliptic problem, degrades more than the velocity or wall shear beside it when the coupling is removed, by 1.8 1.8 – 14.8 × 14.8\times against 1.3 1.3 – 5.0 × 5.0\times . sections.heading: Why the Attention Is Removable and the Coupling Is Not
sections.text: Our aim in this section is to explain the results of Sec. 3 using mathematical theory. Our starting point is the following proposition on the universality of the Transolver layer, Eq. ( 1 ), Proposition 1 (The constant-core class is universal) . Let Ω ⊂ ℝ d \Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded Lipschitz domain and Ψ † : 𝒳 → 𝒴 \Psi^{\dagger}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} a continuous operator between C s C^{s} or W s , p W^{s,p} spaces of functions on Ω \Omega . Fix G ≥ 1 G\geq 1 and let Ψ A \Psi_{A} be the class of operators realized by a stack of layers of the form ( 1 ) with a constant core A A ( NoTokenAttn ), interleaved with pointwise MLPs of unbounded width. Then, for every compact 𝖪 ⊂ 𝒳 \mathsf{K}\subset\mathcal{X} and ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 there exists an operator Ψ ∈ Ψ A \Psi\in\Psi_{A} satisfying sup u ∈ 𝖪 ‖ Ψ ⁡ ( u ) − Ψ † ​ ( u ) ‖ 𝒴 ≤ ϵ \sup_{u\in\mathsf{K}}\|\Psi(u)-\Psi^{\dagger}(u)\|_{\mathcal{Y}}\leq\epsilon . The proof of this proposition is detailed in Appendix A and is based on the universality of averaging neural operators (ANOs) of Lanthaler et al. (2023) , where the authors show that neural operators of the form, Ψ ⁡ ( u ) ​ ( x ) = Q ⁡ ( σ ⁡ ( ∫ Ω R ⁡ ( u ⁡ ( y ) , y ) ​ 𝑑 y ) , x ) , \Psi(u)(x)\;=\;Q\Big(\sigma\big(\textstyle\int_{\Omega}R(u(y),y)\,\mathrm{d}y\big),\,x\Big), (2) with pointwise MLPs R , Q R,Q already suffice for universal approximation of continuous operators. Setting all slice logits to zero makes s g ≡ 1 / G s_{g}\equiv 1/G a partition of unity, every token becomes the global mean, and Eq. ( 1 ) provides the ANO coupling equation 2 , while the pointwise MLPs supply R R and Q Q , and the construction uses no explicit property of G G . The proposition leads to the following immediate conclusions i) to the best of the authors’ knowledge, it provides the first universality result for the original Transolver architecture as it is straightforward to realize token attention weights to obtain a constant A A in equation 1 , making Transolver universal and ii) the result clearly suggests that using a transformer is not necessary for universal approximation and makes this observation of Sec. 3 unsurprising. We can also explain why pointwise MLPs do not suffice for accuracy as reported in Sec. 3 . To this end, we define Definition 1 (Locality gap) . Hence for every Ψ † \Psi^{\dagger} with δ loc ​ ( Ψ † ) > 0 \delta_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Psi^{\dagger})>0 , the error of MlpOnly is at least δ loc ​ ( Ψ † ) \delta_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Psi^{\dagger}) at every depth and every width. Thus, MlpOnly cannot be universal as long as the operator is not entirely pointwise. Moreover, this is the sense in which the MlpOnly gap is not a capacity deficit that MlpOnly-Wide could close. It also orders the tasks: δ loc \delta_{\mathrm{loc}} is largest for operators with global support, the elliptic pressure problem of low-Mach aerodynamics being the canonical case, and smallest for the short-horizon map of Taylor–Green. Finally, the following proposition is suggestive of some of the other observations of Sec. 3 , Proposition 2 (Nonlocal budgets) . Let c c be the width of the point stream. (i) If Ψ † \Psi^{\dagger} is ϵ \epsilon -approximable by an ANO equation 2 of encoding width J ≤ c − k J\leq c-k , with k k channels carrying the coordinates, then a constant-core stack of layers of the form ( 1 ) attains accuracy ϵ \epsilon for every G ≥ 1 G\geq 1 . (ii) One application of 𝒦 \mathcal{K} in equation 1 transmits at most G ​ c G\,c real functionals of the field, and every point receives a fixed linear image of them. A stack that couples at each of L L layers carries at most L ​ G ​ c L\,G\,c ; SliceOnce carries at most G ​ c G\,c whatever the depth of its token stack; MlpOnly carries 0 0 . The bound is rather loose ( G ​ c ≈ 8 × 10 3 G\,c\approx 8\times 10^{3} here); the size of the penalty comes from a second missing ingredient, the universal pointwise decoder Q Q of equation 2 , which SliceOnce replaces by an affine readout in the tokens with coefficients s g ​ ( x ) s_{g}(x) (Table A.1 in Appendix A summarizes these results).

sections.heading: The bottleneck.
sections.text: After removing attention, a physics-attention sublayer is simply a slice → \to per-token linear map → \to deslice operation, and the coupling is what dominates compute and memory. The currently available eager implementation of Transolver forms the slice weights w ∈ ℝ B × H × N × G w\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times H\times N\times G} explicitly and keeps them for the backward pass. For N N in the millions, this is the dominant activation of the layer and the only per-layer term that also grows with G G , so slice count and depth compete for the same memory budget (Figure 3 (b, c)). Slice and deslice cost O ⁡ ( N ​ G ​ D ) O(NGD) multiply-adds for head width D D , comparable to the pointwise MLPs at G = 32 G{=}32 and most of the layer at G = 1024 G{=}1024 . Hence, our aim in this section is to describe FlashSlice, a much more efficient implementation of the slicing kernel.

sections.heading: Design.
sections.text: FlashSlice never writes w w . Each pass streams over the points in tiles, forms the membership tile in registers, applies it and moves on, and the backward pass recomputes the tile from what was saved: the trade FlashAttention ( Dao et al., 2022 ) makes for softmax attention, applied to a pooling that is not attention. The query is a point, the keys are the G G slot projections, the softmax runs over the slots, and the token state between the passes is H × G × D H\times G\times D floats ( 32 32 KB at our configuration). Two things differ from attention: slice is the transpose of deslice, accumulating per slot over points rather than per point over slots, so each point’s normalizer must be known before its contribution is added; and the temperature τ \tau is learned, its gradient cancelling row by row in exact arithmetic, which makes it the most rounding-sensitive quantity in the layer. Two kernel families sit behind one switch and are chosen by shape. • Single-tile kernels , for G G and D D powers of two in [ 16,128 ] [16,128] , hold the whole slot axis in one tile, so that the softmax over G G never leaves registers and no statistics are stored. Tiles are tuned per G G (carrying the G = 32 G{=}32 table to G = 128 G{=}128 costs up to 40 40 – 80 × 80\times through register spilling); they serve every shape of our accuracy experiments. • G G -blocked kernels , for any G ≥ 1 G\geq 1 and head or value widths up to 256 256 , take the approach of FlashAttention’s backward . One online pass forms the per-point softmax statistics ( m n , l n ) (m_{n},l_{n}) , two floats per point and head, i.e. 2 / G 2/G of w w , and every kernel then recomputes w n ​ g = exp ⁡ ( logit n ​ g − m n ) / l n w_{ng}=\exp(\mathrm{logit}_{ng}-m_{n})/l_{n} one G G -block at a time. A deslice with no statistics in hand runs FlashAttention’s forward instead, an online softmax over G G , and hands its statistics to a tied slice; slice cannot run that loop, since its accumulators live on slots and mix many points, so its programs own a G G -block, stream over N N with the finished statistics, and write partials that the host reduces once. The price is the statistics pass and one more logits recompute per backward, so routing prefers the single-tile kernels wherever they apply. Neither family uses atomics, so two runs are bitwise identical, and both are registered as PyTorch custom operators ( Ansel et al., 2024 ) , which makes the model one compiled graph instead of 34 34 and lets every ablation variant of this paper run through the same kernels. Shapes outside both families ( D > 256 D>256 ) fall back to the eager path with a warning recorded on the model, so that a flag left on cannot silently train a baseline replica.

sections.heading: Relation to Transolver-3.
sections.text: Zhou et al. (2026) also avoid the full N × G N\times G weight tensor, by tiling the points in PyTorch and recomputing each tile under gradient checkpointing; each tile of w w is still written to HBM, and the backward reruns the tile’s whole forward. FlashSlice does the same inside the kernel, where the tile never leaves registers. Their second change, moving the input and output projections to token space by associativity, is orthogonal to ours and composes with it.

sections.heading: Precision.
sections.text: We benchmark FlashSlice under both fp32 and bf16 autocast (Appendix F ). Triton’s default dot uses an fp32 FMA path, which becomes a compute bottleneck as G G grows. We therefore provide several dot-precision levels, all with fp32 accumulation (Table F.1 ). The default uses fp32 dots; under bf16 autocast, tensor cores can be used for the value products and, at the bf16 level, for the logits as well. At the other levels the logits remain in fp32 because the softmax Jacobian amplifies errors in the slice weights. In a 50 50 k-step large- G G training run, bf16 dots tracked a tf32 control throughout training while reducing step time by 3.5 × 3.5\times (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: Summary.
sections.text: Our aim was to present a thorough empirical and theoretical analysis of the widely used Transolver architecture in order to uncover the mechanisms that underwrite its accuracy in operator learning on arbitrary domains. By very careful and controlled ablations on a challenging suite of nine benchmarks in fluid dynamics and industrial aerodynamics, we demonstrated that i) token attention can be completely removed and replaced by a constant linear map implying that the Transolver does not require a Transformer ii) the slicing/deslicing global mixing operators are the key source of accuracy and removing them leads to collapse in performance as pointwise MLPs cannot recover global operators and iii) repeating slicing/deslicing in every layer is necessary. We use the theory of averaging neural operators to explain all these findings, providing a clear understanding of the causal mechanisms for Transolver’s function. Finally, we provide a novel and significantly more efficient implementation of the slicing operator by proposing FlashSlice as a computational kernel.

sections.heading: Related Work.
sections.text: Transolver was originally proposed in Wu et al. (2024) and several extensions have been provided by ( Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Adams et al., 2025 ) , among others. The focus of most of these papers is on modifications of the token attention module of Transolver in order to improve performance. On the other hand, there is very little literature on the analysis and understanding of the model itself with the notable exception of Hu et al. (2026) , who observe that the physics-attention is a special case of linear attention and find that deleting the slice attention often improves accuracy on six standard PDE benchmarks. However, they attribute this fact to the tying of the projections, and propose LinearNO, which unties the projections and removes the attention; Yang et al. (2026) reach a compatible reading from a low-rank-kernel viewpoint. As argued in Sec. 3 , we also investigate this claim and this is clearly not the case. Rather, tying is orthogonal to the redundancy of the attention: with or without it, removing the attention costs nothing measurable, and all four cells of Figure 2 (a) lie within 1.05 % 1.05\% of one another. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, our paper is the first to provide theoretical justifications of the extensive empirical findings, leading to a holistic understanding of the mechanisms that govern Transolver’s behavior.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work.
sections.text: Our paper focuses on one, albeit very widely used, neural operator architecture and the findings about the role of global mixing vs. attention might not carry over to other unrelated neural operators. Moreover, our theory is based on model expressivity. It does not take generalization and optimization into account, nor are the bounds sharp. Yet, we could use the theory to suggest hypotheses which were validated with extensive empirical evidence. Going forward, we would like to leverage the insights presented here to develop novel neural operators that have optimized and non-redundant kernels, leading to further accuracy on AI for industrial engineering.

Take the G G slice logits identically zero, so that s 1 = ⋯ = s G ≡ 1 / G s_{1}=\cdots=s_{G}\equiv 1/G , a legal partition of unity reached exactly rather than in a limit. Every normalized token is then the global mean, z h = ( 1 G ​ ∫ Ω v ​ 𝑑 μ ) / ( 1 G ​ | Ω | ) = v ¯ z_{h}=\big(\tfrac{1}{G}\int_{\Omega}v\,\mathrm{d}\mu\big)\big/\big(\tfrac{1}{G}|\Omega|\big)=\bar{v} , and with the constant core scaled so that ∑ g , h A g ​ h / G = 1 \sum_{g,h}A_{gh}/G=1 , Eq. The pointwise MLP sublayers that precede and follow it realize R R and Q Q up to the usual universal approximation of ordinary networks ( Lanthaler et al. 2023 , Lemma A.5, after Pinkus 1999 ), the coordinate x x being available to Q Q through the residual stream, so Theorem 1 applies verbatim. The construction uses no property of G G and is available at every G ≥ 1 G\geq 1 . ∎ Proposition 1 is deliberately not the range argument that a similar claim tempts one to make. It is true, and used in § 2 , that the range of 𝒦 \mathcal{K} is span ​ { s g } \mathrm{span}\{s_{g}\} regardless of A A , so that a content-dependent core cannot enlarge what a single coupling expresses. That alone shows only that the attention cannot enlarge the layer’s range, not that it is dispensable, since a constant and a content-dependent core parameterize different maps within the same range; the density statement is what removes the expressivity-based reason to expect the attention to be necessary. What the proposition does not imply is the stronger reading that the attention therefore costs nothing at the budget a practitioner trains at. Universality is shared by the two classes: NoTokenAttn ’s class is contained in Baseline ’s, both are universal, and this density cannot separate them; and the construction spends unbounded pointwise width, which no experiment has. Universality predicts the absence of a ceiling, not the absence of a cost. That the cost of removing the attention is indistinguishable from zero on nine benchmarks at matched capacity is an empirical finding; the theory makes it unsurprising rather than deriving it from first principles.

sections.heading: The frozen basis.
sections.text: Part (i) uses a constant, non-adaptive basis, s g ≡ 1 / G s_{g}\equiv 1/G fixed once as in FrozenSlice , and still attains universality, because all the adaptivity it needs comes from the pointwise networks between rounds. This matches the ANO itself, whose single nonlocal ingredient is a fixed uniform average. Read literally, it predicts that a frozen basis is not subject to a hard ceiling analogous to MlpOnly or SliceOnce : given enough depth, a fixed basis reused at every layer can still reach any target. What re-estimating { s g } \{s_{g}\} from f ( ℓ − 1 ) f^{(\ell-1)} buys is efficiency: a data-dependent basis can spend each of its L L rounds probing whichever G G -dimensional projection of the current field is most informative, whereas a frozen basis probes the same projections every round and relies on the pointwise nonlinearity between rounds to make each repetition informative. This is the distinction of § A.2 , no ceiling but a cost, and the cost is what Table 1 measures, at a few percent to 17 % 17\% . It also names the discriminating experiment: under a depth sweep the MlpOnly and SliceOnce gaps should persist at every L L , while the FrozenSlice gap should close. We state this as a prediction; the depth sweep is not among the runs we report.

sections.heading: The learned basis, empirically
sections.text: We compare the slice functions learned by independently trained Baseline and NoTokenAttn on DrivAerML. At the last layer, both models produce spatially coherent patterns corresponding to recognizable parts of the car, including the greenhouse and upper body, front fascia, and flanks (Figure A.1 ). Matching slices by cosine similarity over points gives similarities of 0.82 0.82 , 0.72 0.72 , and 0.69 0.69 for the three closest pairs. At the first layer, assignments are nearly uniform in both models: the mean per-point entropies are 3.47 3.47 and 3.46 3.46 nats, close to the maximum ln ⁡ 32 = 3.47 \ln 32=3.47 , and all 32 32 slices are effectively used. The spatial patterns therefore develop in later layers. At the last layer, NoTokenAttn uses more effective slices than Baseline ( 20.4 20.4 vs. 15.4 15.4 ), but has lower mean per-point entropy ( 2.22 2.22 vs. 2.48 2.48 nats). Thus, it uses more slices overall while making more concentrated assignments at individual points. This is consistent with the interpretation in § A.4 : when the core is held constant, the learned basis may take on a greater role in input-dependent routing. sections.heading: Model.
sections.text: The baseline uses a Transolver backbone with 8 8 layers, hidden width 256 256 , 8 8 heads, 32 32 slices, an MLP ratio of 2 2 , GELU activations, and no dropout (approximately 3.87 3.87 M parameters). sections.heading: The Untied-LN variant.
sections.text: For Untied-LN , we use the released layer implementation of Hu et al. (2026) , integrated without changes into our training framework (Appendix E ). Relative to the baseline, this layer gives deslicing its own projection and temperature, removes token self-attention, and normalizes the analysis weights with a separate softmax over the N N points (Figure E.1 (a)). The last change distinguishes Untied-LN from combining Untied and NoTokenAttn , which normalizes the per-point slice weights by their sums over points. sections.heading: Pointwise predictions on aerodynamic benchmarks
sections.text: A pointwise model receives the input features at each query point, including freestream conditions where provided (Table B.1 ), but cannot combine information across points. Local geometric features, such as surface normals and signed distance, do not generally determine the surrounding flow: the field also depends on the rest of the body. This dependence remains when the inflow is fixed but the geometry varies between samples. Consistent with this, the largest MlpOnly error increase occurs on DrivAerML, which uses fixed inflow, rather than on the varying-inflow SHIFT-Wing benchmark (Table 1 ). On the DrivAerML example in Figure D.1 , MlpOnly smooths the wheel-arch suction and front stagnation patterns, with errors around the wheels, mirror, and A-pillar. The per-variable results in Figure 2 (d) show a larger relative error increase for pressure than for velocity or wall shear across the aerodynamic benchmarks. These observations are consistent with a loss of information about the overall geometry. SliceOnce shows a different distribution of errors across fields, suggesting that its limitations are not fully explained by the pointwise model’s lack of spatial coupling. For SHIFT-Wing, pressure errors are computed using dimensional pressure, whose large ambient offset ( p ∞ ≈ 23.8 p_{\infty}\approx 23.8 kPa) dominates the denominator. sections.heading: Appendix E LinearNO implementation and latent width
sections.text: For the Untied-LN variant in Figure 2 (a), we use the released layer implementation of Hu et al. (2026) within the same model framework as Transolver. The lifting MLP, pre-layer normalization, residual connections, and output head are unchanged, so the comparison isolates the replacement of the attention layer. This experiment uses one seed on SHIFT-SUV surface.

sections.heading: Normalization.
sections.text: Both layers aggregate point features into tokens and map the tokens back to points, but construct their aggregation weights differently (Figure E.1 (a)). Transolver applies a softmax over the G G slices at each point and uses the resulting weights in both directions. Each aggregated token is then divided by the sum of its weights over points. LinearNO uses separate weights for slicing and deslicing. Its deslice weights q q are normalized over latent channels, whereas its slice weights k k are normalized over points. The released implementation explicitly stores both tensors, each of shape [ B , H , N , M ] [B,H,N,M] , where M M is the latent width per head. Their memory footprint therefore grows linearly with M M . For Transolver, FlashSlice avoids materializing the corresponding point-to-slice weights (§ 5 ). sections.heading: Appendix F FlashSlice: implementation and evaluation
sections.text: This appendix describes the kernels, numerical validation, and performance measurements supporting § 5 . Experiments use a node with four NVIDIA GH200 GPUs ( 95 95 GB usable HBM per GPU), PyTorch 2.5, and Triton 3.0 ( Ansel et al., 2024 ; Tillet et al., 2019 ) . Unless stated otherwise, measurements use one GPU with C = 256 C=256 , H = 8 H=8 , G = 32 G=32 , L = 8 L=8 , and batch size 1 1 . Each comparison is measured within the same job using fixed seeds and at least ten timed iterations after warm-up. We report median times; observed min–max spreads are below 2 % 2\% . Point counts are rounded in the tables. The main sweep uses powers of two from 2 18 2^{18} to 2 24 2^{24} , with additional intermediate sizes near the memory limit.

sections.heading: Single-tile kernels.
sections.text: For each head, the slice operation computes w i ​ g = softmax G ⁡ ( x mid , i ​ W ⊤ + b τ ) g , z g num = ∑ i w i ​ g ​ f i , s g = ∑ i w i ​ g . w_{ig}=\operatorname{softmax}_{G}\left(\frac{x_{\mathrm{mid},i}W^{\top}+b}{\tau}\right)_{g},\qquad z_{g}^{\mathrm{num}}=\sum_{i}w_{ig}f_{i},\qquad s_{g}=\sum_{i}w_{ig}. The normalized tokens are z g = z g num / ( s g + ε ) z_{g}=z_{g}^{\mathrm{num}}/(s_{g}+\varepsilon) . Deslicing recomputes the weights and maps the mixed tokens back to points. When the slice axis fits within a tile, the softmax is computed locally for each point. The weights remain in registers rather than being written to HBM, and are recomputed during backward. Reductions use fp32 partial buffers followed by a deterministic tree reduction without atomics. The kernels read the projections in their native ( N , H , D ) (N,H,D) layout, avoiding the eager implementation’s layout copies. Input projections remain separate GEMMs, and the token transformation remains in PyTorch. In a forward-only comparison over 36 tile configurations, fusing the projections achieved only 0.18 0.18 – 0.75 0.75 times the throughput of separate cuBLAS projections followed by the kernel. The single-tile implementation supports power-of-two D D and G G in [ 16,128 ] [16,128] , with value width equal to D D . Other supported shapes use the G G -blocked kernels; D > 256 D>256 falls back to eager execution with a warning. Tile settings are tuned separately for each G G . The forward and backward kernels are registered as PyTorch custom operators with shape inference and autograd support, allowing the tested model to compile as a single graph.

sections.heading: G G -blocked kernels.
sections.text: For larger or irregular slice counts, the kernels process the slice axis in blocks of G B G_{B} . A statistics pass computes the maximum logit m n m_{n} and the shifted exponential sum l n l_{n} for each point and head. Subsequent kernels reconstruct weights blockwise as w n ​ g = exp ⁡ ( a n ​ g − m n ) l n , w_{ng}=\frac{\exp(a_{ng}-m_{n})}{l_{n}}, where a n ​ g a_{ng} is the temperature-scaled logit. Slice programs own a block of slots and reduce over points, producing partial token numerators and weight sums. Column normalization is applied after these partials have been combined. Deslice programs own a block of points and reduce over slots. When statistics are unavailable, deslicing uses an online softmax reduction and saves ( m , l ) (m,l) for reuse. Operations with the same membership weights can share these statistics. Backward uses separate point-owned and slot-owned kernels. The point-owned kernel makes two passes over slots to compute the softmax correction and input gradients. The slot-owned kernel accumulates projection, bias, and token gradients over points. This requires more logit recomputation than the single-tile implementation. The blocked family therefore uses its own tile settings, with G B G_{B} selected from 16 16 – 64 64 according to the dot-product tile size.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.32525v1 [cs.LG] 26 Sep 2026 Does Transolver really need a Transformer? Shizheng Wen Siddhartha Mishra Affiliation: Seminar for Applied Mathematics, ETH Zurich, Switzerland Affiliation: {shizheng.wen, siddhartha.mishra}@sam.math.ethz.ch Affiliation: Code: https://github.com/Shizheng-Wen/flashslice Abstract The widely used Transolver family of neural operators is based on physics-attention, which softly assigns the points of an unstructured mesh to a small number of slices, applies self-attention among the resulting tokens, and broadcasts the result back to the points. We provide a comprehensive empirical and theoretical analysis to elucidate the mechanisms which are responsible for model performance. To this end, we perform careful ablations on a challenging suite of nine 3D fluid dynamics benchmarks to find that replacing token attention with a constant linear map does not affect the accuracy. Thus, Transolver does not need a Transformer at all. However, removing the global mixing (slicing/deslicing) or doing it only once leads to performance collapse. We leverage the theory of averaging neural operators to explain and corroborate our findings by showing that just slicing/deslicing, in conjunction with pointwise MLPs, already suffices for universal approximation of continuous operators and attention is redundant in this context. Finally, we provide a novel FlashAttention-style efficient implementation of the key slicing/deslicing module of Transolver. This FlashSlice kernel streams slice and deslice over the points without materializing the heavy slice-weight tensor, while reproducing the best available implementation to floating point error. At the same time, it leads to very significant memory and compute savings, particularly at large slice counts. Introduction Partial differential equations (PDEs) describe diverse phenomena across the physical sciences and engineering ( Evans, 2010 ) , and simulating them accurately is a central task of computational science. Classical numerical methods ( Quarteroni & Valli, 1994 ) do so reliably, but a high-fidelity simulation of a flow around an industrial geometry can occupy an HPC cluster for hours to days. This cost becomes prohibitive in the many-query settings of design optimization, uncertainty quantification and inverse problems, where the same equation is solved for thousands of geometries and operating conditions. Scientific machine learning ( Mishra & Townsend, 2024 ) , in the specific form of operator learning , addresses this bottleneck by learning the solution operator of a PDE from a dataset of simulations, so that a new instance costs a very cheap single forward model pass. The first generation of operator learning algorithms was designed for structured grids: the Fourier neural operator ( Li et al., 2021 ) , DeepONet ( Lu et al., 2021 ) , convolutional neural operators ( Raonić et al., 2023 ) and operator vision transformers ( Herde et al., 2024 ) are based on Cartesian grids. Industrial engineering simulations, however, are based on unstructured meshes and point clouds that can resolve localized features such as boundary layers, shocks and vortices at widely varying point densities. A growing literature targets this setting with graph neural networks ( Pfaff et al., 2021 ; Mousavi et al., 2026 ) , geometry-informed hybrids ( Li et al., 2023b ; Wen et al., 2025 ) and transformers whose tokens are mesh point features ( Cao, 2021 ; Hao et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023a ) . Among the latter, Transolver ( Wu et al., 2024 ) has become a widely used choice. Its physics-attention layer softly assigns each of the N N mesh points to a small number G G of slices , computes self-attention among the G G resulting tokens, and broadcasts the result back to the original points, at a cost linear in N N . It has been extended by Transolver++ ( Luo et al., 2025 ) , Transolver-3 ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) and GeoTransolver ( Adams et al., 2025 ) , among others, and adopted in industrial frameworks such as NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo. Despite its popularity, we argue that the Transolver model itself has not been properly analyzed and understood. In particular, which of its three ingredient operations: slicing/deslicing, attention among the tokens and persistent pointwise MLPs, is responsible for the accuracy shown by the model is completely unclear. Although the focus of successive works on Transolver has been to modify the attention mechanism, it is not even clear whether Transolver really needs a Transformer inside it or not? or whether memory-heavy operations such as slicing/deslicing contribute significantly to its accuracy. Our main motivation for this paper is to perform a comprehensive empirical and rigorous mathematical analysis of the Transolver model to precisely answer such questions. In this regard, our contributions in this paper are, Figure 1: What Transolver’s accuracy does, and does not, need. (a) A Transolver layer: a persistent full-resolution point stream, coupled through slice and deslice with shared per-point slice weights w w to H × G H{\times}G tokens that are re-formed at every layer. Each ablation is drawn on the element it changes; w ( 1 ) w^{(1)} denotes the layer- 1 1 weights reused by FrozenSlice and w ′ w^{\prime} the separate deslice weights of Untied . FlashSlice: The Reduced Layer as a Kernel The bottleneck. After removing attention, a physics-attention sublayer is simply a slice → \to per-token linear map → \to deslice operation, and the coupling is what dominates compute and memory. The currently available eager implementation of Transolver forms the slice weights w ∈ ℝ B × H × N × G w\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times H\times N\times G} explicitly and keeps them for the backward pass. For N N in the millions, this is the dominant activation of the layer and the only per-layer term that also grows with G G , so slice count and depth compete for the same memory budget (Figure 3 (b, c)). Slice and deslice cost O ⁡ ( N ​ G ​ D ) O(NGD) multiply-adds for head width D D , comparable to the pointwise MLPs at G = 32 G{=}32 and most of the layer at G = 1024 G{=}1024 . Hence, our aim in this section is to describe FlashSlice, a much more efficient implementation of the slicing kernel. Design. FlashSlice never writes w w . Each pass streams over the points in tiles, forms the membership tile in registers, applies it and moves on, and the backward pass recomputes the tile from what was saved: the trade FlashAttention ( Dao et al., 2022 ) makes for softmax attention, applied to a pooling that is not attention. The query is a point, the keys are the G G slot projections, the softmax runs over the slots, and the token state between the passes is H × G × D H\times G\times D floats ( 32 32 KB at our configuration). Two things differ from attention: slice is the transpose of deslice, accumulating per slot over points rather than per point over slots, so each point’s normalizer must be known before its contribution is added; and the temperature τ \tau is learned, its gradient cancelling row by row in exact arithmetic, which makes it the most rounding-sensitive quantity in the layer. Two kernel families sit behind one switch and are chosen by shape. • Single-tile kernels , for G G and D D powers of two in [ 16,128 ] [16,128] , hold the whole slot axis in one tile, so that the softmax over G G never leaves registers and no statistics are stored. Tiles are tuned per G G (carrying the G = 32 G{=}32 table to G = 128 G{=}128 costs up to 40 40 – 80 × 80\times through register spilling); they serve every shape of our accuracy experiments. • G G -blocked kernels , for any G ≥ 1 G\geq 1 and head or value widths up to 256 256 , take the approach of FlashAttention’s backward . One online pass forms the per-point softmax statistics ( m n , l n ) (m_{n},l_{n}) , two floats per point and head, i.e. 2 / G 2/G of w w , and every kernel then recomputes w n ​ g = exp ⁡ ( logit n ​ g − m n ) / l n w_{ng}=\exp(\mathrm{logit}_{ng}-m_{n})/l_{n} one G G -block at a time. A deslice with no statistics in hand runs FlashAttention’s forward instead, an online softmax over G G , and hands its statistics to a tied slice; slice cannot run that loop, since its accumulators live on slots and mix many points, so its programs own a G G -block, stream over N N with the finished statistics, and write partials that the host reduces once. The price is the statistics pass and one more logits recompute per backward, so routing prefers the single-tile kernels wherever they apply. Our aim was to present a thorough empirical and theoretical analysis of the widely used Transolver architecture in order to uncover the mechanisms that underwrite its accuracy in operator learning on arbitrary domains. By very careful and controlled ablations on a challenging suite of nine benchmarks in fluid dynamics and industrial aerodynamics, we demonstrated that i) token attention can be completely removed and replaced by a constant linear map implying that the Transolver does not require a Transformer ii) the slicing/deslicing global mixing operators are the key source of accuracy and removing them leads to collapse in performance as pointwise MLPs cannot recover global operators and iii) repeating slicing/deslicing in every layer is necessary. We use the theory of averaging neural operators to explain all these findings, providing a clear understanding of the causal mechanisms for Transolver’s function. Finally, we provide a novel and significantly more efficient implementation of the slicing operator by proposing FlashSlice as a computational kernel. Related Work. Transolver was originally proposed in Wu et al. (2024) and several extensions have been provided by ( Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Adams et al., 2025 ) , among others. The focus of most of these papers is on modifications of the token attention module of Transolver in order to improve performance. On the other hand, there is very little literature on the analysis and understanding of the model itself with the notable exception of Hu et al. (2026) , who observe that the physics-attention is a special case of linear attention and find that deleting the slice attention often improves accuracy on six standard PDE benchmarks. However, they attribute this fact to the tying of the projections, and propose LinearNO, which unties the projections and removes the attention; Yang et al. (2026) reach a compatible reading from a low-rank-kernel viewpoint. As argued in Sec. 3 , we also investigate this claim and this is clearly not the case.
